newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Hong Kong's "Chyuppies" cling to Good Life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hong Kong's "Chyuppies" cling to Good Life.

text.p: A new-generation army of Asian white-collar professionals runs boom-time Hong Kong, a tough nut for China to crack if it abandons a pledged "hands off" attitude and chooses repression.
Aged about 20 to 45, these shock-troops of Hong Kong's middle-class revolution are lawyers, bankers, traders and computer experts in one of the world's most wired-up cities.

They want the good times to keep rolling when the red flag of motherland China replaces the British Union Jack over Hong Kong -- a territory of 6.4 million where the average per capita income is US$25,000 a year.
Beijing has promised to preserve the capitalist way of life for 50 years, but uncertainty lingers.
Columns of "Chyuppies" (Chinese, young, upwardly mobile persons) wear smart designer clothes to work in offices in skyscrapers that have been glacially air-conditioned to beat Hong Kong's humid heat.
They buy management manuals and collect glitzy brand-name consumer goods from shopping mall boutiques.
For them British colonialism, now in its final month, scarcely exists.
It was a harder reality for their parents who lived in a political vacuum under benign but unrepresentative British masters. There was never an ethnic Chinese governor.
PROGNOSIS SEEMS GOOD BUT SUCCESS NOT ASSURED
The new bourgeois-liberal class is wary, like a patient facing unavoidable surgery. The prognosis seems good, but success can't be assured.
"I'm happy now about the changeover," says Kitty Lam, a 35-year-old freelance writer of computer manuals and former public relations executive.
"But I certainly won't wait till 2047 to make up my mind. I'll give it two years and if it doesn't work out I'll move abroad."
Kitty has a lavish lifestyle, a huge apartment, and an Italian boyfriend. She has a Portuguese passport, having been born in Macau, and takes regular holidays abroad.

Eric Ching, who sells computers and offers training courses and customised business software, says: "I think the prosperity of Hong Kong will continue. I see a lot of opportunities with the handover."
"There will not be any drastic changes here. It should be OK, it should be all right," said a 30-something official with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank.
"BUSINESS AS USUAL BUT UNDER DIFFERENT MANAGER"
The aide, who did not wish to be identified, said: "It will be business as usual, but under a different manager."
For decades, Britain and China had a tacit understanding to limit democracy in Hong Kong to avoid any prospect of independence demands, which neither side wanted.
People instead had almost unlimited economic freedom, so that Hong Kong became a Mecca for hard-working fortune seekers, many refugees from mainland turmoil.

Now the sons and daughters of an era with sex-equality, prosperity and job opportunities have tasted some democracy in the last few years with limited reforms introduced by departing governor Chris Patten.
China, which takes back the territory from Britain on July 1, has vowed to scrap these measures, meaning that civil liberties will be reduced.

Pro-democracy activists, backed by Western countries, are locked in a war of words with China-anointed future Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa who regularly reflects Beijing's concern to keep Hong Kong free of "foreign subversion."
CIVIL SERVANTS SEE THEMSELVES AS BULWARK OF EFFICIENCY

Senior administrators in Hong Kong's British-trained 180,000-strong army of civil servants see themselves as a bulwark of efficiency against any disorder that would provoke direct intervention by Beijing.
"Yes, I think we are in the front line of democracy," says K.B. Wong, 40-year-old district officer and part-time magistrate.
He is effectively chief executive of picturesque Cheung Chau island, which has just staged the last major grassroots ballot before the Beijing takeover.
"Democracy will continue. Most people think that. We are confident, especially if we do a good job."
